item.title: DRAG-Inspired Single Flux Quantum Control of Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Long shot new method — Simulated Yπ/2 coherent-control infidelity falls below 10−4 with computational subspace leakage suppressed via DRAG-inspired framing ramps, requiring only a 16-bit stored ramp sequence and 223 Josephson junctions.

Grade 0.430 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “scaling up: crossbar addressing, cryo-CMOS control, qubit interconnects” · V. Vozhakov, M. Bastrakova, A. Liniov, D. Kulandin, N. Klenov, I. Soloviev

Figure

State evolution and pulse trains for Yπ/2 gates using unramped, symmetric-ramped, and independently optimized ramped SFQ sequences, demonstrating leakage elimination into state |2⟩.

Asks

Can coherent errors and leakage intrinsic to discrete SFQ transmon control be suppressed to the level of high-fidelity microwave control while drastically cutting cryogenic memory overhead?

Before

Full SFQ arbitrary sequences required storing hundreds of pulses, while experimental multichip SFQ control had Clifford errors around 1.2(1)% (Liu 2023) and on-chip digital control achieved 99% to 99.9% fidelity (Kang 2024).

But

Purely coherent unitary simulations; ignores relaxation (T1), dephasing (T2), and quasiparticle poisoning. Complete circuit-level timing-closure and layout margins not analyzed.

Tools

Genetic algorithm optimization · Time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulation · Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital logic · Weakly anharmonic Kerr oscillator model

Abstract

Scalable control remains a major challenge for superconducting quantum processors due to the wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity associated with conventional microwave-based architectures. A framework for qubit control based on Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital electronics is presented. For transmon qubits, optimized control sequences are constructed from regular pulse trains framed by arbitrary subsequences (ramps), enabling DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime through genetic-algorithm optimization. For representative Y_(π/2) gates, the resulting sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below 10⁻⁴, including leakage from the computational subspace. The objective of the proposed approach is to demonstrate that coherent errors intrinsic to SFQ control can be reduced to a comparable level for a more scalable cryogenic control architecture. Memory requirements are reduced by storing only the optimized ramps, while a modular controller architecture supporting both regular and arbitrary pulse generation is proposed. The logical complexity of this architecture is estimated from the Josephson-junction counts of its constituent SFQ cells. The proposed approach therefore combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures.

item.title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
item.description:
Long shot new method — Demonstrates statistical quantum phase estimation on an analog simulator without auxiliary qubits, extracting absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in one- and two-dimensional arrays of up to N=19 Rydberg atoms.

Grade 0.412 · 1.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Hendrik Timme, Benjamin F. Schiffer, Ohad Lib, Shijia Sun, Maximilian Ammenwerth, Dominik S. Wild, J. Ignacio Cirac, Immanuel Bloch, Johannes Zeiher

Figure

Measured ground-state energy EGS/(NΩ) and separation to the first excited band versus detuning Δ/Ω for 5- and 19-atom chains, extracted from the Fourier transform of the reconstructed complex Loschmidt echo.

Asks

Can quantum phase estimation and complex-valued Loschmidt echoes be realized on an analog quantum simulator without controlled time evolution or ancilla registers?

But

Operates within the nearest-neighbor Rydberg blockade approximation (Vnn≫Ω,|Δ|); systematic phase error is 𝒪(τ2) after analytical initial-time bias subtraction, requiring nonzero echo amplitude.

Tools

Strontium-88 optical tweezer arrays · Clock-to-Rydberg transition (n=47 ³S₁) · Digital-analog imaginary-time evolution (ITE) protocol · Loschmidt echo phase reconstruction via Cauchy-Riemann relation · Statistical quantum phase estimation

Abstract

Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

item.title: Non-ergodic Area Scaling of Andreev Transport in Al/AlO_x/Al Tunnel Junctions
item.description:
Long shot new result — Subgap Andreev transport in transmon-scale Al/AlOx/Al junctions is non-ergodic and dominated by ≲300 leaky channels with transparencies orders of magnitude above the ideal tunneling limit ≲10−6. For small or high-aspect-ratio junctions, effective transparency τe grows with area instead of averaging out, peaking near Ajj≈0.15 μm2 before decaying as Ajj−1 above a threshold length scale.

Grade 0.402 · 1.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “materials-limited loss: two-level systems, interfaces, valley splitting” · David J. Perello, Marco Coraiola, Minje Park, Cliff Chen, Hanho Lee, Abhishek Banerjee, Gil Refael, Yuki Sato

Figure

Measured normal-state conductance Gn, effective transparency τe=I2/I1, and effective channel number Ne versus junction area Ajj. Unlike linear Gn, τe increases monotonically with area for high-aspect-ratio junctions and peaks non-monotonically near 0.15 μm2 for square junctions before scaling downward as Ajj−1.

Asks

Does the transparency distribution of Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junctions self-average with junction area, ensuring an area-independent current-phase skew?

Before

Assumed constant and independent of area Ajj when isolating higher Josephson harmonics from circuit inductance in transmons.

But

Measured on 134 devices at T=10 mK in the zero-temperature limit kBT≪Δ; σII≲0.14 nm is bounded algebraically from above rather than uniquely resolved.

Tools

subgap DC transport spectroscopy · shadow evaporation · order-statistics modeling · Monte Carlo simulations

Abstract

State-of-the-art superconducting qubits rely on Al/AlO_x/Al Josephson junctions (JJs) as a nonlinear element with an ideal sinusoidal current-phase dependence, with its inductance set by the junction area and oxidation conditions. This idealization holds only if the many conduction channels through the amorphous AlO_x barrier transmit weakly and almost identically. Here, we measure the second-order subgap Andreev current, which sets the second Josephson harmonic, in Al/AlO_x/Al JJs. For junction sizes relevant to qubits, we find that this current is dominated by lesssim300 effective channels whose transparencies exceed the ideal tunneling limit (lesssim10⁻⁶) by orders of magnitude. For small and high-aspect-ratio junctions, increasing the junction size does not average out the effect of these high transparency channels but instead adds additional channels of even greater transparency. The trend inverts once both the width and length of the junction exceed a critical length scale, above which the effective transparency decreases with area. This non-ergodic scaling of the Andreev current is reproduced by simulations and attributed to non-self-averaging statistics of the transparency distribution, which arise from variations in oxide thickness. The effect is largely invisible to the normal-state conductance used to target the inductance and reveals unexpected geometric and size-related trade-offs for scaling superconducting qubit systems to large numbers of junctions.
